notes:
Bar Magnet as a Dipole

  • Magnetic moment $m = q_m(2l)$, where $q_m$ is pole strength; unit A m$^2$.
  • Field on axial line: $B_{axial} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3}$; on equatorial line: $B_{eq} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{r^3}$ (for $r\gg l$) — exactly analogous to the electric dipole with $\varepsilon_0 \leftrightarrow 1/\mu_0$.
  • Torque in a uniform field: $\tau = mB\sin\theta$; potential energy $U = -mB\cos\theta$.

Earth's Magnetism

  • Earth behaves like a magnetic dipole tilted about $11.3^\circ$ from the geographic axis, with its magnetic south pole near geographic North.
  • Three elements: declination $\theta$ (angle between geographic and magnetic meridian), dip/inclination $\delta$ (angle field makes with horizontal), horizontal component $B_H = B\cos\delta$; vertical component $B_V = B\sin\delta$; $\tan\delta = B_V/B_H$.
  • At the magnetic equator, $\delta = 0$; at the magnetic poles, $\delta = 90^\circ$ and $B_H = 0$.

Magnetisation & Magnetic Intensity

  • Magnetic intensity $H$ (due to free currents); magnetisation $M$ = net magnetic moment per unit volume; $B = \mu_0(H+M)$; susceptibility $\chi = M/H$; permeability $\mu = \mu_0\mu_r = \mu_0(1+\chi)$.

Classification of Magnetic Materials

Type$\chi$$\mu_r$BehaviourExamples
Diamagneticsmall, negativeslightly $<1$weakly repelled; no dependence on temperature (mostly); field lines expelledBi, Cu, water, NaCl
Paramagneticsmall, positiveslightly $>1$weakly attracted; $\chi \propto 1/T$ (Curie's law)Al, Na, O$_2$, CuCl$_2$
Ferromagneticlarge, positive$\gg1$strongly attracted; retains magnetism; domains; loses ferromagnetism above Curie temperature and becomes paramagneticFe, Co, Ni
  • Hysteresis: retentivity (residual $B$ at $H=0$) and coercivity (reverse $H$ needed to bring $B$ to 0). Permanent magnets need high retentivity & coercivity (steel); electromagnets need low coercivity & high permeability (soft iron).

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 1–2 questions here — one on the dia/para/ferromagnetic comparison table (very fact-based, high scoring) and one numerical/conceptual on dipole field or Earth's magnetic elements ($\tan\delta = B_V/B_H$). Quick, easy marks if the table is memorised.

questions.q: A bar magnet of magnetic moment $m$ produces a magnetic field $B_1$ at a point on its axial line at distance $r$. The field at the same distance on the equatorial line is
questions.explanation: $B_{axial} = 2\times(\mu_0/4\pi)(m/r^3)$ and $B_{eq} = (\mu_0/4\pi)(m/r^3)$, so $B_{eq} = B_{axial}/2$.
questions.trick: Bar magnet: equatorial field is always half the axial field, same as electric dipole.

questions.q: The magnetic dipole moment of a bar magnet of pole strength 5 A m and length 10 cm is
questions.explanation: $m = q_m\times2l = 5\times0.1 = 0.5$ A m$^2$.
questions.trick: $m=q_m\times2l$ — plug pole strength and full length directly.

questions.q: At a place, the angle of dip is $45^\circ$. If the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field is $0.3$ G, the vertical component is
questions.explanation: $\tan\delta = B_V/B_H \Rightarrow B_V = B_H\tan45^\circ = 0.3\times1 = 0.3$ G.
questions.trick: $\tan45^\circ=1$, so $B_V=B_H$ — a freebie whenever dip is $45^\circ$.

questions.q: At the magnetic poles of the Earth, the angle of dip and the horizontal component of the field are respectively
questions.explanation: At the poles the field is vertical, so dip $\delta=90^\circ$ and $B_H = B\cos90^\circ = 0$.
questions.trick: At poles: field is fully vertical, so dip $=90^\circ$ and $B_H=0$ always.

questions.q: A diamagnetic material placed in a magnetic field
options: retains magnetism after the field is removed
gets strongly magnetised along the field
gets weakly magnetised opposite to the field
questions.explanation: Diamagnetic substances acquire a weak magnetisation opposite to the applied field (negative susceptibility) and are repelled from stronger field regions.
questions.trick: Diamagnetic = weakly magnetised OPPOSITE to field, never retains it.

questions.q: The susceptibility of a paramagnetic substance varies with absolute temperature $T$ as
questions.explanation: Curie's law: $\chi = C/T$, so paramagnetic susceptibility decreases as temperature increases.
questions.trick: Curie's law: $\chi\propto1/T$ — paramagnetism weakens as temperature rises.

questions.q: Above the Curie temperature, a ferromagnetic material becomes
questions.explanation: Thermal agitation destroys the domain alignment above the Curie point, and the material behaves as an ordinary paramagnet.
questions.trick: Above Curie point, ferromagnetic $\to$ paramagnetic, always — domains break down.

questions.q: Which of the following has relative permeability slightly less than 1?
questions.explanation: Diamagnetic materials like copper have small negative susceptibility, so $\mu_r = 1+\chi$ is slightly less than 1.
questions.trick: $\mu_r$ slightly under 1 = diamagnetic signature — copper is the classic example.

questions.q: For making a permanent magnet, the material should have
questions.explanation: A good permanent magnet (e.g. steel) must retain strong magnetism (high retentivity) and resist demagnetisation (high coercivity).
questions.trick: Permanent magnet needs HIGH retentivity AND HIGH coercivity — both high.

questions.q: For an electromagnet core, the material chosen should have
options: high permeability and low retentivity/coercivity (like soft iron)
questions.explanation: Soft iron has high permeability (magnetises easily and strongly) but low retentivity/coercivity, so it loses magnetism as soon as current is switched off — ideal for electromagnets.
questions.trick: Electromagnet core needs high permeability but LOW retentivity/coercivity — soft iron.

questions.q: The relation between magnetic field $B$, magnetic intensity $H$ and magnetisation $M$ is
questions.explanation: By definition, $B = \mu_0(H+M)$ in a magnetised medium.
questions.trick: $B=\mu_0(H+M)$ — memorise this exact defining relation, no other form.

questions.q: A magnetic needle free to rotate in a horizontal plane aligns itself along the direction of
options: the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field
the total magnetic field of the Earth
the vertical component of Earth's magnetic field
questions.explanation: A compass needle constrained to a horizontal plane experiences only $B_H$, so it aligns along the magnetic meridian defined by the horizontal component.
questions.trick: Free horizontal needle aligns with $B_H$ only — vertical component has no effect.

questions.q: The angle between the geographic meridian and the magnetic meridian at a place is called
questions.explanation: Declination is the angle between true (geographic) north and magnetic north at a place.
questions.trick: Declination = angle between geographic and magnetic meridian; dip is the vertical tilt.

questions.q: Gauss's law for magnetism, $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0$, over any closed surface implies
options: magnetic field lines always form closed loops (no isolated poles)
questions.explanation: Zero net flux through any closed surface means magnetic field lines never start or end at a point (no monopole); they form closed loops.
questions.trick: Zero net magnetic flux through any closed surface = no monopoles, only closed loops.

questions.q: A bar magnet of length 5 cm and magnetic moment 1 A m$^2$ is placed with its axis along an external field of 0.2 T. The work done to rotate it by $90^\circ$ from this position is
questions.explanation: $W = U(90^\circ)-U(0^\circ) = -mB\cos90^\circ-(-mB\cos0^\circ) = 0+mB = 1\times0.2 = 0.2$ J.
questions.trick: Rotating from $0^\circ$ (aligned) to $90^\circ$: work done is simply $mB$.

questions.q: A short bar magnet has magnetic moment $2$ A m$^2$. The magnetic field at a point on its equatorial line at a distance of 0.1 m is
questions.trick: $B_{eq}=(\mu_0/4\pi)(m/r^3)$ — use $10^{-7}$ for $\mu_0/4\pi$ directly.

questions.q: Curie temperature of iron is about 1000 K. Below this temperature iron is ferromagnetic mainly because
options: iron has zero magnetic moment per atom
iron is diamagnetic at low temperature
individual atomic dipoles are aligned randomly
domains (regions of aligned atomic moments) exist and can be aligned by an external field
questions.explanation: Ferromagnetism arises from domains — regions where atomic magnetic moments are already aligned; an external field aligns the domains themselves, giving a large net magnetisation.
questions.trick: Ferromagnetism = pre-existing domains that external field ALIGNS, not creates.

questions.q: If the horizontal component of Earth's field at a place is 0.24 G and the angle of dip is such that $\tan\delta = 1.5$, the vertical component is
questions.explanation: $B_V = B_H\tan\delta = 0.24\times1.5 = 0.36$ G.
questions.trick: $B_V=B_H\tan\delta$ — direct multiplication, no need for $B$ itself.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches material type with susceptibility sign?
questions.explanation: Paramagnetic materials have small positive $\chi$ (weakly attracted); diamagnetic materials have small negative $\chi$ (weakly repelled).
questions.trick: Sign rule: paramagnetic $\chi>0$ (attracted), diamagnetic $\chi<0$ (repelled).

questions.q: A magnetic compass needle placed at the magnetic equator of the Earth will point
questions.explanation: At the magnetic equator, dip $\delta=0^\circ$, so the Earth's field is entirely horizontal and the needle aligns horizontally along the magnetic meridian.
questions.trick: At magnetic equator, dip $=0^\circ$: field is purely horizontal, needle lies flat.

questions.q: The SI unit of magnetic pole strength ($q_m$) is
questions.explanation: Since $m=q_m(2l)$ and $m$ has unit A m$^2$ while $2l$ is in metres, $q_m$ must have unit A m.
questions.trick: $q_m$ unit: A m, since $m=q_m\times2l$ needs A m$^2$ / m.

questions.q: A bar magnet is equivalent to a solenoid of $N$ turns, area $A$, carrying current $I$. Its magnetic moment is
questions.explanation: The equivalent solenoid model gives magnetic moment $m = NIA$, exactly like a current loop's dipole moment.
questions.trick: Equivalent solenoid model: $m=NIA$, same formula as a current loop's moment.

questions.q: A circular coil of 100 turns and radius 10 cm carries a current of 0.5 A. Its magnetic moment is approximately
questions.explanation: $m = NI\pi r^2 = 100\times0.5\times\pi\times(0.1)^2 = 50\times0.0314 = 1.57$ A m$^2$.
questions.trick: $m=NI\pi r^2$ — treat coil as current loop, use $\pi r^2$ for area.

questions.q: A rectangular coil of 50 turns and area 0.02 m$^2$ carrying a current of 2 A is placed with its plane parallel to a magnetic field of 0.1 T. The torque on the coil is
questions.explanation: With plane parallel to $B$, the normal is perpendicular to $B$ so $\sin\theta=1$: $\tau = NIAB = 50\times2\times0.02\times0.1 = 0.2$ N m.
questions.trick: Plane parallel to $B$ → $\sin\theta=1$: torque is simply $\tau=NIAB$.

questions.q: In a vibration magnetometer, a magnet of moment 0.3 A m$^2$ and moment of inertia $3\times10^{-6}$ kg m$^2$ oscillates with a period of 2 s in a magnetic field $B$. The value of $B$ is approximately
questions.explanation: $T=2\pi\sqrt{I/(mB)} \Rightarrow B = \dfrac{4\pi^2I}{mT^2} = \dfrac{4\pi^2\times3\times10^{-6}}{0.3\times4} \approx 1\times10^{-4}$ T.
questions.trick: $T=2\pi\sqrt{I/mB}$ — rearrange for $B=4\pi^2I/(mT^2)$, standard SHM analogy.

questions.q: An electron revolves in a circular orbit around the nucleus. The magnetic moment associated with its orbital motion is directed
options: opposite to the orbital angular momentum vector, since the electron is negatively charged
along the direction of orbital velocity
along the orbital angular momentum vector
questions.explanation: The orbital current is opposite to the electron's velocity (negative charge), so the associated magnetic moment vector points opposite to the orbital angular momentum vector.
questions.trick: Electron's orbital moment is ANTIPARALLEL to angular momentum (negative charge flips it).

questions.q: Which of the following statements about diamagnetic susceptibility is correct?
options: It is large and positive, increasing with temperature
It becomes zero above the Curie temperature
It is small and negative, and nearly independent of temperature
questions.explanation: Diamagnetism arises from induced currents opposing the field and is a small, negative, essentially temperature-independent effect, unlike paramagnetism which follows Curie's law.
questions.trick: Diamagnetic $\chi$: small, negative, and temperature-independent — unlike Curie's law for paramagnets.

questions.q: A superconductor placed in a magnetic field expels the field completely from its interior (Meissner effect). Its relative permeability and susceptibility are respectively
questions.explanation: A superconductor is a perfect diamagnet: $B=0$ inside means $\mu_r=0$, so $\chi=\mu_r-1=-1$.
questions.trick: Superconductor (Meissner effect): perfect diamagnet, $\mu_r=0$, so $\chi=-1$ exactly.

questions.q: A bar magnet is placed with its north pole pointing geographic north. Neutral points (where the resultant magnetic field is zero) are obtained
options: on the axial line of the magnet
on the equatorial line of the magnet, where the magnet's field cancels the Earth's horizontal field
nowhere, since the fields never cancel
at the poles of the magnet itself
questions.explanation: With the N pole pointing north, the magnet's equatorial field (which points opposite to its own axis, i.e. southward) can cancel the northward $B_H$ of the Earth, giving neutral points on the equatorial line.
questions.trick: Neutral points with N pole facing north always form on the EQUATORIAL line.

questions.q: Inside a bar magnet, the magnetic field lines run from
options: there are no field lines inside a magnet
N pole to S pole, same as outside
S pole to N pole, forming closed loops with the external field lines
questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines have no beginning or end; outside a magnet they go from N to S, and inside they continue from S back to N, forming closed loops (consistent with $\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec A=0$).
questions.trick: Field lines inside a magnet go S to N, closing the loop with outside N to S.

questions.q: In a tangent galvanometer experiment, the horizontal component of Earth's field is balanced against the field due to current in the coil. If the deflection is $\theta$, the relation used is
questions.explanation: The needle settles along the resultant of the coil's field $B$ (perpendicular to $B_H$) and $B_H$ itself, so $\tan\theta = B/B_H$, giving $B=B_H\tan\theta$ (tangent law).
questions.trick: Tangent law: $B=B_H\tan\theta$ — coil field is perpendicular to $B_H$ by design.

questions.q: Two short magnets of moments 3 A m$^2$ and 4 A m$^2$ are placed with their axes perpendicular to each other. The resultant magnetic moment is
questions.explanation: For perpendicular vectors, resultant $=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=\sqrt{25}=5$ A m$^2$.
questions.trick: Perpendicular moments combine via Pythagoras: $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$.

questions.q: The value of the permeability of free space $\mu_0$ is
questions.explanation: $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T m/A (or H/m) by definition in SI units.
questions.trick: $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T m/A — pair with $k=9\times10^9$ as the two constants to memorise.

questions.q: The area enclosed by the hysteresis loop (B-H curve) of a magnetic material represents
options: the maximum magnetisation of the material
the energy dissipated as heat per unit volume per cycle of magnetisation
questions.explanation: Work is done against the internal friction of domain realignment during each magnetisation cycle; this lost energy per unit volume equals the loop's enclosed area.
questions.trick: Hysteresis loop area = energy lost as heat per unit volume per cycle, always.

questions.q: Compared to soft iron, the hysteresis loop of steel is
options: absent, since steel shows no hysteresis
fatter, with larger retentivity and coercivity, hence larger hysteresis loss
questions.explanation: Steel has high retentivity and coercivity (good for permanent magnets) but this means a fatter loop and greater hysteresis loss compared to soft iron, which has a thin loop suited to electromagnets.
questions.trick: Fatter hysteresis loop = more retentivity/coercivity = more loss — that's steel vs soft iron.

questions.q: An electron moves in a circular orbit of radius $5\times10^{-11}$ m with speed $2\times10^{6}$ m/s. The equivalent magnetic moment due to its orbital motion is
questions.explanation: Equivalent current $I=\dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}$, so $m=I\pi r^2=\dfrac{evr}{2}=\dfrac{1.6\times10^{-19}\times2\times10^6\times5\times10^{-11}}{2}=8\times10^{-24}$ A m$^2$.
questions.trick: Orbiting charge as current loop: $m=evr/2$ — derive from $I=ev/2\pi r$ and $A=\pi r^2$.

questions.q: Which of the following is a ferromagnetic material?
questions.explanation: Nickel, along with iron and cobalt, is ferromagnetic; aluminium and sodium are paramagnetic while bismuth is diamagnetic.
questions.trick: Only Fe, Co, Ni are ferromagnetic — memorise this short list to eliminate options fast.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes ferromagnetic from paramagnetic behaviour?
options: Ferromagnetic susceptibility is small and constant, like paramagnetic
Ferromagnetic susceptibility is large, positive and varies non-linearly with $H$, unlike the small, nearly constant susceptibility of paramagnetic materials
Paramagnetic materials show hysteresis while ferromagnetic materials do not
questions.explanation: Ferromagnetic materials have large, field-dependent (non-linear) positive susceptibility due to domain alignment, and show hysteresis, unlike the small, nearly constant susceptibility of paramagnets.
questions.trick: Ferromagnetic $\chi$ is large, non-linear with $H$, and shows hysteresis — paramagnetic doesn't.

questions.q: A bar magnet of magnetic moment $m$ and length $2l$ is cut into two equal pieces by a cut perpendicular to its length. The magnetic moment of each piece is
questions.explanation: Each piece has the same pole strength $q_m$ but half the length ($l$ instead of $2l$), so its moment is $q_m l = m/2$.
questions.trick: Cut perpendicular to length: pole strength unchanged, length halves, so $m\to m/2$.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A diamagnetic material has no permanent (net) magnetic dipole moment of its own. Reason (R): In a diamagnetic material, the applied field induces a magnetic moment that opposes the field. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Diamagnetic atoms have no net intrinsic dipole moment (paired electrons); the field itself induces a small opposing moment, which is exactly why A is true and R correctly explains it.
questions.trick: Diamagnetic atoms: zero intrinsic moment; field induces the small opposing moment.
